Key Message 1...Seasonably warm with a few spotty showers and 
thunderstorms this weekend.

Surface high pressure near the Canadian Maritimes extends westward 
along the New England coastline today. An axis of moisture within an 
area of convergence extends from the Mid-Atlantic region into 
western NY this afternoon. A mid-level trough will move across the 
region through tonight, and the axis of moisture will move eastward 
across the forecast area. Partly to mostly cloudy conditions and a 
few showers and thunderstorms are possible along and inland from the 
Lake Erie lakebreeze this afternoon. Decreasing chances for showers 
and cloud coverage will move eastward across the Genesee Valley and 
Finger Lakes region through early this evening.

As clouds move east of the region, clearing is expected across the 
western Southern Tier tonight. Patchy fog is possible and result in 
low visibility late tonight into Sunday morning. 

Increasing moisture will move into the eastern Great Lakes region 
ahead of the next shortwave trough Sunday. Daytime heating and lake 
breeze and terrain circulations will support a chance of a few 
showers and thunderstorms inland from the Lakes Sunday afternoon 
through early evening. Hi-res guidance suggest an area of numerous 
showers and thunderstorms from the Toronto Metro to the Niagara 
Peninsula in the afternoon which may move into the Buffalo/Niagara 
Falls Metro Sunday evening. 

Daytime highs will reach the low to mid 80s today and Sunday and 
overnight lows in the upper 50s to mid 60s tonight and Sunday night.

Key Message 2...More unsettled weather will return Monday and 
Tuesday with increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms. 

A large upper-level ridge will remain anchored across the southern 
Rockies Monday and Tuesday. Downstream...a broad longwave trough 
will also remain in place from eastern Canada to the Great Lakes/New 
England...while being reinforced by several shortwave impulses 
riding around the top of the ridge and then dropping through the 
mean northwesterly flow aloft. As these latter features cross our 
region and interact with our seasonably warm and increasingly more 
humid airmass...we should experience increasingly unsettled weather 
featuring periodic rounds of showers and scattered thunderstorms. 

Coupled with diurnal heating/destabilization...an initial shortwave 
impulse crossing our region should lead to an increasing likelihood 
of some showers and scattered storms inland from the lakes during 
Monday afternoon...particularly across our central and eastern zones 
where available moisture should be a bit deeper and forcing from the 
shortwave looks to be maximized. Meanwhile a relative minimum in 
convective coverage should lie northeast of Lake Erie...where a 
stabilizing southwesterly flow off that lake looks to be in place. 
With respect to severe potential on Monday...at this point this 
appears fairly limited given the weak low-mid level flow and 
consequently fairly weak shear in place across much of the region... 
meaning that localized heavier downpours may actually be the main 
concern instead given the weak flow and PWATs of up around 1.5 
inches. This being said...deep-layer shear is a bit stronger (25-30 
knots) across the western Southern Tier...so can't completely rule 
out a couple of stronger storms there.

Increasingly more widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms 
then look to arrive Monday night (mainly later on in the night) and 
Tuesday as another...stronger shortwave impulse and associated 
surface wave drop southeastward across the Great Lakes and across 
our region...though the exact track/timing of these features still 
remain in question at this juncture. The latest suite of guidance 
continues to suggest that the best overall convective coverage 
should come during Tuesday afternoon/evening in tandem with diurnal 
heating/destabilization...though available shear again looks to be 
largely weak and unsupportive of an organized severe risk. This 
said...the one exception to this could again be across the Southern 
Tier... which will lie along the northeastern edge of faster flow/ 
better shear sliding across the Ohio Valley/Mid-Atlantic...and where 
a few stronger storms can once again not be completely ruled out. 
Otherwise PWATs will remain around or a little above 1.5 inches 
during this time frame...which should lead to a continued potential 
for locally heavy downpours.

Key Message 3...A few more showers/storms linger into Wednesday, 
otherwise turning drier through the end of the work week.

Following the passage of the Tuesday system...lingering large-scale 
troughing across our region and daytime heating underneath its 
attendant cool pool aloft should lead to another round of diurnally-
driven convection developing inland from the lakes during Wednesday.
